tagline.text: A hilltop cultural village of Ifugao houses and art galleries

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–600 (including admission, snacks and a portrait sketch, per person)

children.text: Tam-awan Village is an art village on a hill in Pinsao, northwest of Baguio, where traditional Cordillera houses have been rebuilt, and it opened in 1998. You can see Ifugao and Kalinga houses, galleries, a café, a sunset viewpoint and traditional dance performances in one place, and you can even spend the night in a hut.

Tam-awan Village is a cultural and art village in Pinsao Proper, Baguio City. "Tam-awan" means "vantage point" in the local language, and the village was built on land that was once cattle pasture with a spring. It was opened in 1998 by the non-profit Chanum Foundation, with help from the National Artist BenCab, who wanted to nurture local artists. You tour the village with the map and brochure you receive at the entrance, and if you sign up for a guided tour, you can hear explanations of the artworks.
The village began with the restoration of Ifugao houses, so that people could experience the living culture of the mountain provinces without traveling all the way to the Cordillera. The roughly
2.5 ha

grounds have seven Ifugao houses and two Kalinga houses, rebuilt by local craftsmen with wooden pegs, rattan lashings and cogon roofs. The houses are also smoked in the traditional way to keep termites away.

The Binayon house of southern Kalinga is authentic, and as of 2011 it was described as one of only three left in the country. One house serves as a gallery, and around the village there are the Village Gallery, the Bugnay Gallery, a sketching area and a craft shop. You can also see a traditional Bontoc rice granary and a pond. Some accounts describe certain Ifugao houses as "fertility huts," with a belief that touching the idols helps you conceive. One house has exhibited Jordan Mang-osan's "Solar Drawings," and an exhibit on Ifugao art is ongoing. Exhibits can change, so check before you go.

The village sits on a steep hill, and narrow paths lead up through it. From the house at the top you can look down on the village and part of Baguio, and many visitors praise the sunset on clear days. It is about 20 minutes by car from busy downtown Baguio, so it fits well into a half-day outing. Inside the village, meter-wide dirt paths branch in several directions, and the brochure you get at the entrance has a map. There are also a hanging bridge, a trellised path and resting huts, which make the walk enjoyable.
Seven Ifugao houses and two Kalinga houses stand along the hill. They are built with wooden pegs, rattan lashings and cogon roofs, and visitors call the village a "living museum."
The Village Gallery has a wild boar installation by Hilario Quirona, and the Bugnay Gallery shows paintings by Filipino artists. One house is used as an exhibition space.
Village artists sketch portraits of visitors. You must sit as a model for about
10–20 minutes

. In 2023 the price was about ₱100 for a solo black-and-white sketch, about ₱150 in color, about ₱300 for two people in black and white and about ₱350 in color, though some recent accounts mention about ₱200 per person.
There are performances of Igorot traditional dances. Check the show schedule with the village before you visit.
From the viewpoint on the hill you can watch the sun set in the west, and on clear days you reportedly see as far as the West Philippine Sea. Arriving around
and staying until sunset is recommended.
One suggested route around the village ends by crossing a bamboo bridge. Along the paths there are also a hanging bridge and a resting hut.
The café in the village serves Cordillera-style drinks and snacks. Visitors often say the prices are reasonable.
You can stay one night in a traditional hut. Which huts are available varies with the season, so confirm when you book.

Watch the sunset from the viewpoint and, once the sun has set, return to town by taxi.
Jeepney and taxi availability varies from day to day, so decide in advance how you will get back before dark.
Long-distance buses such as Victory Liner run to Baguio from Cubao, Pasay and other Manila terminals. The trip usually takes
4.5–5.5 hours
and a one-way ticket costs about
If you drive, take NLEX and TPLEX up to Baguio. The village is northwest of downtown, so you still have to travel further from the city center.
Bus times and fares change, so check the operator's latest announcements.
On Kayang Street near Baguio Market, board a jeepney marked "Long Long Road" or "Tam-awan." As of 2023 the fare was reported to be about
For a taxi, tell the driver "Tam-awan, Pinsao Proper." With good traffic it takes about
20 minutes
Coming back, you need to flag down a passing jeepney or taxi, so it is safer to head down before dark. Check the route signs and fares locally.
The road to the village is steep and winding, so drive with care.
The Igorot Stone Kingdom and a restaurant called Farmer's Daughter are close by.

You can visit the village all year round, but the dry season from November to May is better for walking. When it rains the paths turn muddy and slippery, and visitors are advised to avoid rainy days. Baguio is at altitude and stays cool even at midday, so an afternoon outing is not a burden.
During the Panagbenga Flower Festival in February the town is crowded, so the quiet of the village can feel all the more welcome. To see the sunset, arrive around
on a clear day.

The Tam-awan Café inside the village serves Cordillera-style coffee, snacks and simple meals. One review reported a sandwich at about ₱130. The village is known for its communal table, where you are told you can sit with the artists over coffee and chat. Check the on-site rules on bringing outside food. The café reportedly serves Cordillera-style smoked pork as a drinking snack, and sets up a place where visitors share coffee or the traditional drink "tagay" with the artists. You can order afternoon snacks while you wait or relax.

Lodging is in huts inside the village. According to a 2020 guide, the rate was ₱500 for one person, ₱1,000 for two and ₱300 for each extra person, and groups of ten or more paid ₱350 each. Available huts and prices may change, so confirm when you book.

A 2011 trip report described the huts available for overnight stays as Anaba, Love Bug, Dukligan, Lukkong and New Hut. They have basic amenities only and no cable TV, and larger groups pay less per person. Visitors praise the view of the village and part of Baguio from the hut at the top.
Before you go, check the opening hours and fees with the village's official website or contact details. The email is listed as tamawanvillage@gmail.com and the phone number as (074) 446-2949.

Respect Cordillera culture, and do not touch the houses or statues carelessly.
